Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z) = z-y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u^2, \: -v, \: v \big\rangle
$$

for $(u,v) \in D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where $u \geq 0.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \| = 2\sqrt{2}u.$*" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d27e0ee0-ad93-5416-8abb-f21167765a8b" "question-f95319f6-2e43-511b-ae0d-9608a991c217"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-2c7beff7-ff72-566b-ae77-d272cca30605" :question/id #uuid "2c7beff7-ff72-566b-ae77-d272cca30605" :question/math-academy-id "q-161288" :question/problem "$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=-x-{z}^{2}$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{3},\,v,\,{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3{u}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-6v{u}^{2})^{2}+(3{u}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{v}^{2}{u}^{4}+9{u}^{4}} \\  & =3{u}^{2}\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x={u}^{3}\,y=v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =-{u}^{3}-({v}^{2}\cdot {v}^{2}) \\  & =-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,3{u}^{2}(-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4})\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-72a815fc-9d19-53b2-b0ae-b65abcc40317"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & ={u}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2\sqrt{2}{u}^{2}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-16fadbea-4516-5df4-9f64-8b7cc353d5a0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-16fadbea-4516-5df4-9f64-8b7cc353d5a0" :answer-field/id #uuid "16fadbea-4516-5df4-9f64-8b7cc353d5a0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b146a4db-c677-57ea-92f8-07f41239596d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b146a4db-c677-57ea-92f8-07f41239596d" "answer-c87217ff-e3d3-5223-ac71-463a0c197918" "answer-b723dafe-f5a6-5a70-be14-953187b88dde" "answer-e4f2c71c-8604-5aa1-9ce7-1663a5f2e6db" "answer-31c23b1e-7cd7-5e7a-8c99-254c33c9229b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b146a4db-c677-57ea-92f8-07f41239596d" :answer/id #uuid "b146a4db-c677-57ea-92f8-07f41239596d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}{u}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c87217ff-e3d3-5223-ac71-463a0c197918" :answer/id #uuid "c87217ff-e3d3-5223-ac71-463a0c197918" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{u}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b723dafe-f5a6-5a70-be14-953187b88dde" :answer/id #uuid "b723dafe-f5a6-5a70-be14-953187b88dde" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{u}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e4f2c71c-8604-5aa1-9ce7-1663a5f2e6db" :answer/id #uuid "e4f2c71c-8604-5aa1-9ce7-1663a5f2e6db" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-31c23b1e-7cd7-5e7a-8c99-254c33c9229b" :answer/id #uuid "31c23b1e-7cd7-5e7a-8c99-254c33c9229b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{v}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172377 :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u-v,\,3u+2,\,u+2v⟩
$$

 
over the domain $D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{70}.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{70}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(2x+y+z)\,{|}_{x=2u-v\,y=3u+2\,z=u+2v} \\  & =2(2u-v)+(3u+2)+(u+2v) \\  & =8u+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(8u+2)\sqrt{70}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}{∬}_{D}\,(8u+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{70}{\int }_{0}^{1}(8u+2)\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot [4{u}^{2}+2u]_{0}^{1}\cdot [u]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{70}\cdot 6\cdot 2 \\  & =12\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be382d30-f02e-5329-bcf7-16808280a34b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-be382d30-f02e-5329-bcf7-16808280a34b" :answer-field/id #uuid "be382d30-f02e-5329-bcf7-16808280a34b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7d00c43b-e899-573d-afa8-6b12ead91cda" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7d00c43b-e899-573d-afa8-6b12ead91cda" "answer-bc8100ab-c718-514d-8f3c-f28643c256a5" "answer-6ed83581-5e32-5a0e-8a25-178bb99cade4" "answer-d24b3aff-8b91-5bf0-8ab1-f276e0780c98" "answer-11345332-1583-5403-b382-1f7db9544110"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7d00c43b-e899-573d-afa8-6b12ead91cda" :answer/id #uuid "7d00c43b-e899-573d-afa8-6b12ead91cda" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12\sqrt{70}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc8100ab-c718-514d-8f3c-f28643c256a5" :answer/id #uuid "bc8100ab-c718-514d-8f3c-f28643c256a5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{70}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6ed83581-5e32-5a0e-8a25-178bb99cade4" :answer/id #uuid "6ed83581-5e32-5a0e-8a25-178bb99cade4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "36\sqrt{70}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d24b3aff-8b91-5bf0-8ab1-f276e0780c98" :answer/id #uuid "d24b3aff-8b91-5bf0-8ab1-f276e0780c98" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\sqrt{70}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-11345332-1583-5403-b382-1f7db9544110" :answer/id #uuid "11345332-1583-5403-b382-1f7db9544110" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{70}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-d27e0ee0-ad93-5416-8abb-f21167765a8b" :question/id #uuid "d27e0ee0-ad93-5416-8abb-f21167765a8b" :question/math-academy-id "q-161181" :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

r(u,v)=⟨2u+v,\,2u+v,\,-v⟩
$$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3x-2y+3z)\,{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u+v\,z=-v} \\  & =3(2u+v)-2(2u+v)+3(-v) \\  & =2(u-v)\end{aligned}

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-93abc2ba-af03-5472-9cce-10fe847607a0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-93abc2ba-af03-5472-9cce-10fe847607a0" :answer-field/id #uuid "93abc2ba-af03-5472-9cce-10fe847607a0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e1fe1620-65f9-5859-8a82-9a5f97b2fafb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e1fe1620-65f9-5859-8a82-9a5f97b2fafb" "answer-44291a57-8b30-555c-b7e9-95314ffa4f9d" "answer-38973f90-0f85-5e71-8380-79a67500ceed" "answer-22129875-cc14-5ad3-8bba-b26995c05188" "answer-ab922d47-0766-574c-83bb-4e4ccfbb77ca"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1fe1620-65f9-5859-8a82-9a5f97b2fafb" :answer/id #uuid "e1fe1620-65f9-5859-8a82-9a5f97b2fafb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-44291a57-8b30-555c-b7e9-95314ffa4f9d" :answer/id #uuid "44291a57-8b30-555c-b7e9-95314ffa4f9d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38973f90-0f85-5e71-8380-79a67500ceed" :answer/id #uuid "38973f90-0f85-5e71-8380-79a67500ceed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-22129875-cc14-5ad3-8bba-b26995c05188" :answer/id #uuid "22129875-cc14-5ad3-8bba-b26995c05188" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ab922d47-0766-574c-83bb-4e4ccfbb77ca" :answer/id #uuid "ab922d47-0766-574c-83bb-4e4ccfbb77ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f95319f6-2e43-511b-ae0d-9608a991c217" :question/id #uuid "f95319f6-2e43-511b-ae0d-9608a991c217" :question/math-academy-id "q-161179" :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=3\sqrt{6}.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.

If our surface is "sufficiently smooth," we can define the **surface integral** of $f$ over $S.$ Let's discuss how we might construct such an integral.

For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that our region $D$ is rectangular. We start by creating a partition $P$ of $D$ in the usual way:

$$
P = \left\{u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_m\right\} \times \left\{v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n\right\}
$$

Our partition is shown schematically below.

![](images/6a/6a15c7b587503c82a57d0734c5bc5fda990824ad162724236868461cd92e4fbe.png)

 

The area $\delta A = \delta u\delta v$ of the small rectangle highlighted in the diagram corresponds to a particular patch $S_{ij}$ of area $\delta S_{ij}$ on our surface. 

![](images/1a/1a8774b7aa366d3328b6f81cfe7315b7784a1f5783f14c1f19f83a459cef5434.png)

 

Let $P_{ij}^*$ be a point on the surface within the patch $S_{ij}.$ We consider the product 

$$
f(P_{ij}^*) \cdot \delta S_{ij}.
$$

If we compute this product for all patches and add them together, we get the Riemann sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f(P_{ij}^*)\cdot\delta S_{ij}.
$$

Taking the limit as $\delta u, \delta v\to 0$ gives our definition of the surface integral of $f$ over $S,$ which we denote as

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S.
$$

From previous discussions, we know that the area of the small patch can be approximated as follows:

$$
\delta S_{ij} \approx \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta u\delta v = \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta A
$$

It follows that we can calculate our surface integral using the following formula:

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A
$$

This formula is also valid when $D$ is non-rectangular. 

Let's see an example of applying this in practice." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173252 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface integral of the function

$$

$$

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}

$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172188 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

$$

Our partition is shown schematically below.

![](images/6a/6a15c7b587503c82a57d0734c5bc5fda990824ad162724236868461cd92e4fbe.png)

Let $P_{ij}^*$ be a point on the surface within the patch $S_{ij}.$ We consider the product 

$$

$$

If we compute this product for all patches and add them together, we get the Riemann sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f(P_{ij}^*)\cdot\delta S_{ij}.
$$

Taking the limit as $\delta u, \delta v\to 0$ gives our definition of the surface integral of $f$ over $S,$ which we denote as

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z) = z-y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u^2, \: -v, \: v \big\rangle
$$

for $(u,v) \in D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where $u \geq 0.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \| = 2\sqrt{2}u.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \| = 2\sqrt{2}u.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(z-y)\,{|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=-v\,z=v} \\  & =v-(-v) \\  & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4\sqrt{2}uv\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048384} {:db/id 17592186172375 :question/id #uuid "25e44fde-444d-5880-ba2e-43dd4bc039db" :question/math-academy-id "q-160711"} {:db/id 17592186172376 :question/id #uuid "a99cdea7-3ae5-5a3e-abca-eaac3de706cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-160712" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172130 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5256297-c928-54e3-bf4d-35f5734f5632" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a6318e5-3878-5d26-b61b-739d349729a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2({u}^{2}+u)v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186275566} {:answer/id #uuid "2913e3a7-4834-5ae0-8725-8cf0ddd19bbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2({u}^{2}+uv+{u}^{2})v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186275848} {:answer/id #uuid "4635f4d0-2e93-54c6-a194-c7414540fea3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186276098} {:answer/id #uuid "8e7629cd-993c-5b5b-a5b5-4827bb2f0380" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186276769} {:answer/id #uuid "fa861672-33f6-547e-b490-0aa338df3abc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2(u+v)v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186277670}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "0a6318e5-3878-5d26-b61b-739d349729a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2({u}^{2}+u)v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186275566} :answer-field/id #uuid "758915d5-fc00-56c4-ac7b-2a8b40d5ac5f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186277935}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

:knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\iint\limits_{S} (x-y)\: \textrm{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x = u+v, \qquad 
y = u-v, \qquad 
z = v
$$

for $0 \leq u \leq 3$ and $0 \leq v \leq 3.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u+v, \: u-v, \: v\right\rangle.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+4} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =x-y\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u-v\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)-(u-v) \\  & =2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D = \{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 3, \: 0 \leq v \leq 3\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(x-y)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2v\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,2v\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}2v\,\text{d}v\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}1\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{3}\cdot [u]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot 9\cdot 3 \\  & =27\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172377 :question/id #uuid "82d5af65-9d79-5b70-b0f6-be91c0743951" :question/math-academy-id "q-160834" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b529430-3406-506c-b67d-c067dfee44d5" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bea4b28f-ce09-5500-9439-8c3c8b7ee3cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\sqrt{70}" :db/id 17592186169126} {:answer/id #uuid "ce545157-bc0c-5334-bc0e-9135235b5624" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{70}" :db/id 17592186169127} {:answer/id #uuid "d0a0829c-6ceb-5f41-9889-8a865432b8dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12\sqrt{70}" :db/id 17592186169128} {:answer/id #uuid "fd45b78a-7e91-59f5-a92a-3f200b6d2bfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\sqrt{70}" :db/id 17592186169129} {:answer/id #uuid "2581dec6-23e3-515e-92fb-d7811092bcb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "36\sqrt{70}" :db/id 17592186169130}] :answer-field/id #uuid "6fc03f50-c767-57bd-8d63-af287106c460" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186169125}] :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

[{:db/id 17592186173080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173252 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface integral of the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

 
over the parametric surface $S,$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u, \: 2v, \: -u \big\rangle, \quad (u,v)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is the unit square in the $uv$-plane given by

$$
D = \{(u,v) \: | \: 0\leq u\leq 1,\: 0\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

Let's compute the surface integral of $f$ over $S.$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the surface integral of $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "44c6f181-59d4-55f2-b782-d9635d1f8d52" :step/math-academy-id 44238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173081}} {:db/id 17592186173081 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172130 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171710 :question/id #uuid "38dc8ce4-246d-54bd-a400-48c801d9387f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12344"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5256297-c928-54e3-bf4d-35f5734f5632" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048384}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172375} {:db/id 17592186172376} {:db/id 17592186278393} {:db/id 17592186278394} {:db/id 17592186278395} {:db/id 17592186278462} {:db/id 17592186278463} {:db/id 17592186278464}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "c731cc78-fb9c-5b8e-b331-827b3178f676" :step/math-academy-id 44239 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173082}} {:db/id 17592186173082 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171711 :question/id #uuid "fce43073-3f48-5e12-a5c0-ecef3a31a57a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b529430-3406-506c-b67d-c067dfee44d5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172377} {:db/id 17592186172378} {:db/id 17592186235462} {:db/id 17592186278391} {:db/id 17592186278411} {:db/id 17592186278412} {:db/id 17592186278425} {:db/id 17592186278427} {:db/id 17592186278442} {:db/id 17592186278443}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "59e45b34-814a-5cf5-96db-f904f40aca38" :step/math-academy-id 44243} {:db/id 17592186173088 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173256 :tutorial/content "Consider a continuous scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ and a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ defined for $(u,v) \in D,$ where $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ 

If our surface is "sufficiently smooth," we can define the **surface integral** of $f$ over $S.$ Let's discuss how we might construct such an integral.

The procedure is similar to what we've seen before (for example, regarding the line integrals over a curve). 

For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that our region $D$ is rectangular. We start by creating a partition $P$ of $D$ in the usual way:

$$
P = \left\{u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_m\right\} \times \left\{v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n\right\}
$$

Our partition is shown schematically below.

![](images/6a/6a15c7b587503c82a57d0734c5bc5fda990824ad162724236868461cd92e4fbe.png)

The area $\delta A = \delta u\delta v$ of the small rectangle highlighted in the diagram corresponds to a particular patch $S_{ij}$ of area $\delta S_{ij}$ on our surface. 

![](images/1a/1a8774b7aa366d3328b6f81cfe7315b7784a1f5783f14c1f19f83a459cef5434.png)

Let $P_{ij}^*$ be a point on the surface within the patch $S_{ij}.$ We consider the product 

$$
f(P_{ij}^*) \cdot \delta S_{ij}.
$$

If we compute this product for all patches and add them together, we get the Riemann sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f(P_{ij}^*)\cdot\delta S_{ij}.
$$

Taking the limit as $\delta u, \delta v\to 0$ gives our definition of the surface integral of $f$ over $S,$ which we denote as

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S.
$$

From previous discussions, we know that the area of the small patch can be approximated as follows:

$$
\delta S_{ij} \approx \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta u\delta v = \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta A
$$

It follows that we can calculate our surface integral using the following formula:

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A
$$

This formula is also valid when $D$ is non-rectangular.

$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "44c6f181-59d4-55f2-b782-d9635d1f8d52" :step/math-academy-id 44238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173081}} {:db/id 17592186173252 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface integral of the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

 
over the parametric surface $S,$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u, \: 2v, \: -u \big\rangle, \quad (u,v)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is the unit square in the $uv$-plane given by

$$
D = \{(u,v) \: | \: 0\leq u\leq 1,\: 0\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

Let's compute the surface integral of $f$ over $S.$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the surface integral of $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,0,\,2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186173081 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172130 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171710 :question/id #uuid "38dc8ce4-246d-54bd-a400-48c801d9387f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12344"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5256297-c928-54e3-bf4d-35f5734f5632" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048384}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172375} {:db/id 17592186172376} {:db/id 17592186278393} {:db/id 17592186278394} {:db/id 17592186278395} {:db/id 17592186278462} {:db/id 17592186278463} {:db/id 17592186278464}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "c731cc78-fb9c-5b8e-b331-827b3178f676" :step/math-academy-id 44239 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173082}} {:db/id 17592186173082 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172131 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171711 :question/id #uuid "fce43073-3f48-5e12-a5c0-ecef3a31a57a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b529430-3406-506c-b67d-c067dfee44d5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172377} {:db/id 17592186172378} {:db/id 17592186235462} {:db/id 17592186278391} {:db/id 17592186278411} {:db/id 17592186278412} {:db/id 17592186278425} {:db/id 17592186278427} {:db/id 17592186278442} {:db/id 17592186278443}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "59e45b34-814a-5cf5-96db-f904f40aca38" :step/math-academy-id 44243} {:db/id 17592186173256 :tutorial/content "Consider a continuous scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ and a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ defined for $(u,v) \in D,$ where $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ 

If our surface is "sufficiently smooth," we can define the **surface integral** of $f$ over $S.$ Let's discuss how we might construct such an integral.

The procedure is similar to what we've seen before (for example, regarding the line integrals over a curve). 

For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that our region $D$ is rectangular. We start by creating a partition $P$ of $D$ in the usual way:

$$
P = \left\{u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_m\right\} \times \left\{v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_n\right\}
$$

Our partition is shown schematically below.

![](images/6a/6a15c7b587503c82a57d0734c5bc5fda990824ad162724236868461cd92e4fbe.png)

The area $\delta A = \delta u\delta v$ of the small rectangle highlighted in the diagram corresponds to a particular patch $S_{ij}$ of area $\delta S_{ij}$ on our surface. 

![](images/1a/1a8774b7aa366d3328b6f81cfe7315b7784a1f5783f14c1f19f83a459cef5434.png)

Let $P_{ij}^*$ be a point on the surface within the patch $S_{ij}.$ We consider the product 

$$
f(P_{ij}^*) \cdot \delta S_{ij}.
$$

If we compute this product for all patches and add them together, we get the Riemann sum

$$
\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f(P_{ij}^*)\cdot\delta S_{ij}.
$$

Taking the limit as $\delta u, \delta v\to 0$ gives our definition of the surface integral of $f$ over $S,$ which we denote as

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S.
$$

From previous discussions, we know that the area of the small patch can be approximated as follows:

$$
\delta S_{ij} \approx \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta u\delta v = \| \mathbf r'_u \times \mathbf r'_v\|\,\delta A
$$

It follows that we can calculate our surface integral using the following formula:

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A
$$

This formula is also valid when $D$ is non-rectangular. 

Let's see an example of applying this in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "31cee43f-e940-5add-90d5-831ffcaaafc8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7660 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186045463 Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics.
